answer.divergenceLesson: The context-best matches the raw‑power best, showing that early picks should prioritize the strongest absolute card to stay open for later signals.
answer.narrative: With an empty pool you have no color commitment, so you should grab the highest‑power card in the pack; Sylvan Scavenging tops the pack’s win‑rate and fits that rule [SIG-14][SIG-02]. It also counts as a bomb‑type card that can generate early board advantage, aligning with the BREAD priority of bombs over removal or cheap tricks [EVAL-01][EVAL-02]. By taking the best card now you stay flexible and will be able to read the colors that open in later packs [SIG-01].

coach.text: Bigfin Bouncer is a solid 4‑drop creature that hits a decent IWD and is likely a mid‑range bomb, so it fits the “Bomb” priority nicely [EVAL-02]. It isn’t a clear removal pick like Hero’s Downfall, but its higher maindeck rate and comparable win‑rate make it the stronger immediate play in this pack. Staying open is still fine at pick 2, but keep an eye on blue’s curve and removal needs as you draft.

answer.divergenceLesson: The raw-power best and the context-best are the same, showing that taking the strongest absolute card early is correct and also signals that blue is likely open, reinforcing the strategy of staying open before committing.
answer.narrative: Bigfin Bouncer is a solid 4‑mana creature with a good win‑rate and a high maindecked percentage, making it a strong early pick on pure power [SIG-14]. At pick 2 the card appears earlier than typical for a bomb, signaling that blue is still open and you can safely add a second color [SIG-05][SIG-02]. Keeping your options open early is key, so you don’t lock yourself into green before seeing more signals [SIG-01].

coach.text: Ruby Daring Tracker is a solid 2‑drop scout that fits a green‑red aggressive curve and gives you early pressure, making it a good Bomb‑Aggro pick for your current pool. answer.divergenceLesson: The raw‑power best and the context‑best are the same; taking the strongest 2‑drop now follows the “take the best card early” rule and keeps you open for later color decisions.
answer.narrative: Ruby, Daring Tracker is a solid 2‑mana bomb that adds early board presence and works well with Sylvan Scavenging’s green synergies, while still leaving you open to pivot to a green‑red or green‑blue deck later. Picking the top card in the pack for the first five picks follows the signal‑reading guideline to stay flexible before committing to a two‑color pair [SIG-02][SIG-14], and it also satisfies the BREAD priority of a bomb over removal or evasion [EVAL-02][EVAL-01].

coach.text: Eager Trufflesnout is a solid 3‑drop creature that consistently hits the board early and fits the green curve, making it a clear bomb‑type pick at this stage [SIG-02][EVAL-02].

answer.divergenceLesson: The raw‑power best (Eager Trufflesnout) is a solid 3‑drop bomb, but the context‑best is the 2‑drop Wary Thespian because it improves early curve, keeps the deck flexible on green‑red or green‑blue, and avoids over‑committing to a single mid‑cost threat, illustrating the need to balance raw power with deck consistency.
answer.narrative: At pick 4 you’re still in the “stay open” phase, so you want the strongest card overall but also one that fits your developing curve and signals a viable second color. While Eager Trufflesnout is a solid 3‑drop bomb, Wary Thespian gives you a 2‑drop green creature that improves early tempo, lets you stay flexible on a green‑red or green‑blue plan, and avoids over‑loading on a single 3‑mana threat. Taking the 2‑drop also follows the BREAD priority of securing early board presence (Aggro) before committing to bigger bombs, and it respects the curve guideline of keeping many 1‑2‑drop creatures. If later packs open white or more red, you can pivot; otherwise you’ll have a smoother curve and a safer mana base, preventing the common mistake of sticking with an early bomb at the expense of consistency.

coach.text: Involuntary Employment is a 4‑mana sorcery that isn’t a clear bomb and has a low maindecked rate, so it’s a weaker pick than the cheap creature or the higher‑maindecked Angel; you’d be better off taking a creature that improves board presence and early tempo. [EVAL-02] [EVAL-05] [EVAL-11]

answer.divergenceLesson: Involuntary Employment has the highest raw win‑rate, but it doesn’t fit our current curve or mana base; a cheap 1‑drop like Diregraf Ghoul gives early tempo and signals that black is open, making it the better pick for this deck.
answer.narrative: At pick 5 you should pass the red sorcery and take Diregraf Ghoul, a 1‑drop that shores up your early curve and adds a solid aggressive threat. [EVAL-05][CURVE-01] Because you have no black cards yet, the appearance of this cheap black creature is a clear signal that black is still open, letting you pivot to a black‑red or black‑green plan while keeping red as a possible splash. [SIG-05][SIG-06] Holding onto Involuntary Employment would force you into a two‑color deck with limited early pressure and a shaky mana base, which is why raw‑power win rates can be misleading when the card doesn’t mesh with your developing deck. [MISTAKE-01][EVAL-11]

While Luminous Rebuke has the highest win‑rate, its 5‑mana cost and lack of other white cards make it a poor fit for your current green‑red‑blue pool and would push your curve too high [EVAL-02][CURVE-07]. Dazzling Angel is a cheap 3‑drop creature that provides early pressure and keeps you open to either stay in green/red or pivot to white if more signals appear [SIG-14][ARCH-04].

answer.divergenceLesson: The raw-power best and the context-best are the same; a late‑appearing green bomb both signals that green is still open and fits the green‑heavy pool you already have, reinforcing that taking the strongest card early is still correct here.
answer.narrative: At pick 7 you’re just past the window where you grab the absolute strongest card in each pack (SIG‑02) and should start reading signals. The 6‑mana Quilled Greatwurm showing up this late is a classic open‑color signal (SIG‑05), and you already have three green cards, so green is clearly your primary hue. As a bomb it wins games on its own (EVAL‑02) and dovetails with your existing green threats, making it the best choice for your deck’s development.

coach.text: Felidar Savior is a solid 4‑drop but not a bomb; its power level is below the earlier 1‑ and 2‑drops in the pack and it doesn’t give you a clear signal to commit to white yet [EVAL-02][SIG-01]. This follows SIG-14 (evaluate each pick on absolute power) and SIG-06 (a strong late‑passed card signals an open lane), and aligns with EVAL-01 (creatures with evasion rank high in priority).

Bloodfell Caves, despite its high win rate as a land, does not advance your plan and would lock you into a color you don’t need yet. This shows why you should evaluate each pick on absolute power (SIG-14) and prioritize low‑cost threats early (EVAL-05, EVAL-08), following the guideline to take the best card in the first few picks (SIG-02).

Taking the cheap flyer also signals that white is still open, letting you pivot if later packs deliver green or white threats [SIG-06][SIG-04].

answer.divergenceLesson: Ashroot Animist wins the raw-power ranking, but Healer's Hawk fits the current pool better, gives a cheap 1‑drop to smooth the curve, and aligns with the developing green‑white tempo, illustrating that the best statistical pick isn’t always the best contextual pick.
answer.narrative: Healer's Hawk is a 1‑mana creature that shoves early pressure onto the board and plugs the gap in your curve, which is crucial in a green‑white plan that already has several 2‑ and 3‑drops ([EVAL-05], [CURVE-07]). While Ashroot Animist has the highest GIH, green cards are drying up in this pack, a signal that green may be closing and you should consider pivoting away from a pure green focus ([SIG-07]). By taking the cheap white bird you stay flexible, keep your white removal (Luminous Rebuke) and Felidar Savior useful, and you maintain a solid two‑color base without over‑loading your mana (meeting the 8‑source rule for white) ([MANA-01], [MANA-02]). This choice follows the BREAD priority of taking the strongest early drop when the bomb quality isn’t clear ([EVAL-01]), and it shows why evaluating each pick in a vacuum and then fitting it to your evolving deck is essential ([SIG-14]).

coach.text: Loot is a solid bomb: it has the highest IWD and strong maindecking rate, making it the most reliably powerful card in the pack. It also keeps you open to any color, which is ideal at this early stage [SIG-01][EVAL-02].

answer.divergenceLesson: Loot is a solid green bomb, but your pool is already green‑heavy; adding a white 3‑drop improves color balance and deck consistency, so Prideful Parent is the context‑best. The lesson is to prioritize deck cohesion and signal‑based color choices over a single raw‑power pick.
answer.narrative: Loot is a strong midrange bomb, yet you’ve already drafted a suite of green threats and a green removal spell, so green is becoming saturated. Prideful Parent gives you a reliable white creature that fits the 3‑drop curve, adds a second color for removal (Luminous Rebuke) and synergistic white cards, and follows the BREAD priority of a good creature bomb [EVAL-01]. By pack‑2 pick‑3 you should start leaning toward a two‑color plan; the presence of a solid white 3‑drop signals that white is still open, while green is less promising now [SIG-04][SIG-07]. Choosing Prideful Parent keeps your curve low, improves consistency, and lets you lock in a green‑white midrange archetype [ARCH-03][CURVE-01][DECK-06].

Taking a basic land is safe and keeps your mana base flexible without committing to a color, which is exactly what you want this early in the draft [SIG-01].

Taking the land is safe and keeps your mana base flexible, especially since you still lack a reliable source for blue and you’ve already drafted several green and white lands.
